title: Advertising, visual and digital texts
summary: Read images, layout and typography as carefully as words: the conventions of adverts, posters, infographics, websites, social media and comics.

keyterms.definition: A short, memorable phrase associated with a brand or campaign.
The arrangement of text and images on a page or screen, guiding the reader's eye.
The choice and style of fonts, sizes and weights, which carry connotations.
The associations colours carry, e.g. green with nature or red with danger or passion, which vary by culture.
The direction of a figure's look: a direct gaze at the viewer demands engagement; an indirect one invites observation.
A line, real or implied (such as a gaze or arm), that leads the viewer's eye through an image.
How much an element stands out through size, colour, position or contrast.
Text (such as a caption) that fixes the meaning of an image.
An instruction prompting the audience to do something, such as 'Shop now' or 'Donate today'.
A text that presents data or information visually through charts, icons and short text.
The viewpoint of an image: low angles make subjects powerful, high angles vulnerable.
Combining more than one mode, such as words, images, sound and layout, to make meaning.

questions.prompt: A charity poster shows a child looking straight at the viewer. What is the effect of this direct gaze?
options: It makes the viewer feel addressed and personally responsible
It shows the child is unaware of the camera
questions.explanation: A direct gaze creates a 'demand', making the viewer feel personally implicated.

questions.text: A caption that fixes how we interpret an image provides ___.
questions.explanation: The same photo can be read very differently depending on its caption.

questions.prompt: A sports advert photographs an athlete from below against the sky. What does the low camera angle suggest?
questions.explanation: Low angles make subjects loom over the viewer, suggesting dominance and aspiration.

questions.statement: The largest, brightest element in an advert usually has the highest salience.
questions.explanation: Size, colour, contrast and position determine what the eye notices first.

questions.prompt: Match the visual feature to a likely effect.
questions.explanation: Typography and design choices carry connotations just as words do.

questions.prompt: In a poster, a model's outstretched arm points towards the product. What is the arm acting as?
questions.explanation: Vectors are lines that direct attention through the composition.

questions.text: The choice and style of fonts in a text is its ___.
questions.explanation: Serif fonts may feel traditional; rounded sans-serif fonts friendly and modern.

questions.statement: Colour symbolism is identical in every culture.
questions.explanation: White, for example, can connote purity in some cultures and mourning in others.

questions.prompt: In many left-to-right reading cultures, why might an advert place the problem on the left and the product on the right?
options: The eye reads from left to right, so the layout suggests a journey from problem to solution
Products must always be on the right by law
questions.explanation: Layout can create a narrative of 'before' and 'after' following reading direction.

questions.prompt: Order a typical viewing path through a print advert.
items: Most salient image catches the eye
Logo and call to action close the advert
questions.explanation: Adverts are designed to steer attention from hook to action.

questions.prompt: "Taste the sunshine." What makes this slogan effective?
options: Synaesthetic metaphor links the drink to warmth and happiness
questions.explanation: Mixing senses (tasting sunshine) creates an appealing, memorable association.

questions.text: "Download the app today" at the end of an advert is a call to ___.
questions.explanation: Calls to action convert interest into behaviour; they are usually imperatives.

questions.prompt: An infographic on plastic waste uses a single large bottle icon beside tiny human icons. What is the effect?
options: Visual scale dramatises the problem's size
It makes the data impossible to read
questions.explanation: Infographics persuade through visual emphasis, not just data.

questions.statement: Infographics are always neutral because they present data.
questions.explanation: Choices of data, scale, colour and icons frame information and can be highly persuasive.

questions.prompt: Match the digital feature to its function.

pairs.right: Links posts to a shared conversation
Connects to other texts or sources
Adds tone and emotion to short text

questions.explanation: Digital texts are interactive; audiences participate in meaning-making.

questions.prompt: Why is a social media post described as multimodal?
options: It combines words, images, video, emoji and layout to make meaning
It is written in many languages
questions.explanation: Multimodal texts make meaning through several modes at once, so analyse their interaction.

questions.text: A short, memorable phrase linked to a brand is a ___.
questions.explanation: Slogans rely on brevity and sound patterns such as alliteration and rhyme.

questions.prompt: In a comic, a panel with no border that bleeds to the edge of the page often suggests:
options: Expansiveness or a moment outside normal time
questions.explanation: Panel size and borders control pacing and emphasis in graphic texts.

questions.statement: An influencer's casual 'unboxing' video can be analysed as a persuasive advertising text.
questions.explanation: Sponsored content uses an authentic-seeming persona and ethos to sell; recognising this is critical media literacy.

questions.prompt: A perfume advert uses deep red, dim lighting and a woman glancing sideways out of frame. Which reading is best supported?
options: Mystery and seduction are linked to the product
The product is cheap and practical
questions.explanation: Colour symbolism, lighting and an indirect gaze build an aura of allure around the product.
